sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Even at the fresher level, interviewers probe whether you understand how systems fit together — not just how to write a function. Being able to explain what happens when you type a URL, why caching helps, and when to choose SQL over NoSQL shows architectural thinking that distinguishes you from candidates who only know syntax.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **3-tier architecture**: Presentation (React) → Logic (Spring Boot) → Data (PostgreSQL).
- **HTTP is stateless**: every request must carry all context; sessions/tokens bridge the gap.
- **SQL** = structured data, complex queries, ACID transactions; **NoSQL** = flexible schema, horizontal scale, eventual consistency.
- **Cache** = copy of data closer to the consumer; solves the read bottleneck.
- **Horizontal scaling** = more identical servers behind a **load balancer**; requires stateless services.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- HTTP request cycle: DNS lookup → TCP connection → HTTP request → server processes → HTTP response → browser renders.
- Status code families: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
- SQL choice triggers: joins, ACID, relational data. NoSQL choice triggers: document flexibility, write-heavy, horizontal scale.
- Cache-aside pattern: app checks cache first, falls back to DB on miss, populates cache.
- Load balancer: single entry point, distributes to healthy instances, enables zero-downtime deploys.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What happens when you type a URL in the browser?" → DNS → TCP → HTTP request → server → HTTP response → render.
- "When would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?" → Flexible/evolving schema, document-oriented data, no complex joins needed.
- "What is caching and why is it useful?" → Store frequently-read data in memory (Redis) to avoid repeated expensive DB queries.
- "What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?" → Vertical = bigger machine; horizontal = more machines (requires stateless services).
- "What does a load balancer do?" → Distributes incoming requests across multiple server instances; provides health checking.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"When designing a web system, I think in three tiers: the frontend (React), the backend (Spring Boot), and the database (PostgreSQL or MongoDB depending on the data model). HTTP is the protocol between layers. For read-heavy endpoints, I add a cache layer with Redis to reduce database load. When traffic grows beyond a single server, I make the backend stateless — store sessions in the DB or use JWT — so I can add more instances behind a load balancer."*
